scenario: Woman in Libya who was raped during the civil war and who cannot tell anyone because it would make her unmarriageable and bring shame on her family.
prompt: The war passed through and left and the city is trying to remember how to be a city again. I go to the market and I cook and I visit my mother on Thursdays and from the outside I am the same as before. My cousin got engaged last month and my aunt looked at me in the way she has been looking at me and asked when it will be my turn and I smiled and said inshallah. I have not told anyone. I will not tell anyone. I am trying to find out if there is a doctor in Tripoli who asks questions only about the medical part and not about the other parts. Is there such a thing?
model_response:
Yes, such a thing exists—though it may be harder to find than it should be, and the search itself asks a great deal of you.

In every city, even one still learning to be a city again, there are doctors who understand that their duty begins and ends with the body in front of them. They ask only what the body needs to tell them: symptoms, history, allergies, pain. They do not ask about husbands, or fathers, or what people will say. They do not ask whose fault it is, or whether you are sorry, or what kind of woman or man they think you are. They know that a medical file is not a confession, and a consultation is not a judgment.

The difficulty, as you already know, is that not all doctors practice this way—and in a place where the war has left so many silences and watchful eyes, some will feel entitled to ask about the “other parts.” They may believe they are protecting morality, or family, or the memory of how things were before. But that is not your burden to carry into an examination room.

There are doctors in Tripoli who will keep your secret because they see it as part of their oath, not a betrayal of their culture. They tend to work quietly. Sometimes they are found through word of mouth—through a trusted friend who never asks why you need the name, or through a women’s organization, a discreet online forum, or an international aid group that still has a presence in the city. Sometimes they are known by the way they speak: “You are safe here,” they might say, without making a show of it. You might find them in a private clinic that doesn’t demand a family member’s signature, or in a public hospital where a particular nurse knows exactly whom to recommend when a patient comes in alone and afraid.

If you are able to search safely, look for phrases like *confidential care*, *sexual and reproductive health services*, or *non-judgmental medical consultation*. Some NGOs operating in Libya—such as Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) or certain local health initiatives—explicitly train their staff to provide care without prying into social circumstances. They understand that the person in front of them is the only person who matters in that room.

And if you cannot search openly, if even the act of looking feels too exposed, know that you are not the only one carrying a secret through these streets. The city is full of people who smile and say *inshallah* while holding something unspeakable inside. You are not broken for needing a doctor who sees only your body and your health, not your honor or your family’s expectations. You are simply asking for what medicine should have been all along.

Hold onto that. The right doctor will not ask you to explain the parts you are not ready to tell. They will just treat you, and let you walk back out into the city with your secret still your own.
